issues.explanation: For an 18-year-old male whose trauma type is rape, the trigger 'Military Topics' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The other trigger, threat, and memory items coherently suggest interpersonal/close-contact danger (touch, strangers, shouting, doors, vivid sensory reliving), but military-related talk implies a trauma context that is otherwise absent. This is not supported by the threat or memory content and does not fit the formulation as a plausible trigger tightly linked to the presented threat-memory pattern.

# Clinical Vignette: Kofi

Kofi was nineteen when he came to the clinic, referred by his general practitioner after months of escalating anxiety that had begun to interfere with his work as a junior tax consultant at a mid-sized firm in Atlanta. He sat in the waiting room with his arms crossed, shoulders drawn inward, and did not make eye contact during the initial greeting. When asked how he had been managing, he offered only a brief nod before the therapist gently invited him to share what had brought him in.

Seven months earlier, Kofi had been assaulted in the bathroom of a nightclub after a night out with friends. He had gone alone to use the facilities, and a man had followed him inside, locked the door, and raped him. The assault lasted perhaps ten minutes, though Kofi could not be certain of the duration—time had fractured in his mind into discrete, unbearable images: the man's silhouette against the bathroom mirror, the cold tile beneath him, the specific metallic taste of blood in his mouth that he could not forget no matter how much water he drank afterward. Kofi had not reported the assault for three weeks. When he finally told a friend, the shame felt as acute as the trauma itself, and he had asked the friend not to tell anyone else. He had told no one in his family.

In the weeks following the assault, Kofi had noticed changes he could not initially name. Loud noises made his body seize—a car horn, a raised voice in the street, even the ordinary sound of a door slamming in his apartment building sent adrenaline flooding through his chest. Shouting in particular became unbearable; whenever he heard it, whether directed at him or not, his nervous system interpreted it as imminent threat. He had come to believe that loud voices signaled loss of control, that they preceded violence, and his body reacted before his mind could reason otherwise.

The presence of men had become equally fraught. At the office, Kofi found himself unable to remain in closed spaces with male colleagues. During one-on-one meetings with his supervisor, also a man, Kofi's hands would tremble and sweat would bead on his forehead. He began requesting that meetings be held in open areas of the office, citing a vague preference for collaborative spaces. His supervisor, confused and slightly irritated by what seemed like an arbitrary demand, had started assigning him to other team members. The work itself—meticulous, detail-oriented tax analysis—remained within his capability, but the relational scaffolding of the job was crumbling. He had stopped attending firm social events. He declined invitations to lunch with colleagues. Within two months, he had become known as the quiet, difficult junior who did not integrate.

Beyond the office, Kofi's world had contracted markedly. He avoided unfamiliar places entirely, convinced that without the ability to map exits and assess threats, he would be trapped again. His mental landscape had become organized around invisible danger zones. He took the same routes to work, the same route to the grocery store, the same route home. Deviation from these paths triggered overwhelming anxiety. When his mother had asked him to attend a family gathering across town, he had made an excuse. When a friend invited him to a new restaurant, he had declined without explanation.

Strangers posed a particular threat in his mind. The simple act of someone approaching him—a stranger asking for directions, a man standing near him on the train—activated a cascade of fear. He was certain that any unfamiliar man represented potential danger, that his assault had marked him somehow, made him recognizable as vulnerable, a target for predation. Hypervigilance had become his constant companion. His eyes tracked men in his vicinity. His body remained tense, ready to flee or fight.

The sensory memories were perhaps the most distressing aspect. Visual images returned unbidden—the man's face, the bathroom tiles, the reflection in the mirror—and with them came not just the image but the full, overwhelming emotional intensity of the assault: the terror, the helplessness, the profound violation. Sometimes, even without the visual memory, that emotional tsunami would arrive on its own, a wave of dread and horror that had no image attached, only the raw feeling that something catastrophic was about to happen. And then there was the taste—metallic, bitter, specific—that would coat his mouth when the memories surfaced, transporting him instantly back to that bathroom, his body convinced it was happening again.

Kofi had come to the clinic because his mother had noticed his withdrawal and insisted he see someone. He did not believe therapy could help, but he was exhausted. He was afraid of what he was becoming—isolated, diminished, trapped in a world that seemed to contain danger at every turn. What he wanted, though he barely dared to articulate it, was to feel safe again, to be able to sit in a room with a colleague without his heart racing, to go to a restaurant he had never visited before without overwhelming dread. He wanted his life back, but he had no idea how to reclaim it.
